title: Collagen and Alcohol: Does Drinking Undo Your Collagen?
excerpt: Can you take collagen and drink alcohol? How alcohol breaks down your skin's collagen, what collagen supplements can and can't do, whether they help a hangover, and what actually protects your skin.
metaDescription: Can you take collagen and drink alcohol? How drinking affects your skin's collagen, what supplements can really do, and what actually protects your skin.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** taking a collagen supplement and drinking alcohol is not dangerous. There is no known interaction between the two, and collagen does not change how your body handles alcohol. The more useful question is whether drinking undoes what you are taking collagen for, and the answer there is yes, if the drinking is regular and heavy. Alcohol works against your skin's own collagen in several ways: it dehydrates you, drives inflammation and oxidative stress, wrecks sleep, and drains the nutrients your body needs to build new collagen. A scoop of collagen powder can't outrun a habit of several drinks a night.

This guide explains what collagen actually is, how alcohol affects it, what the research on collagen supplements really shows, whether collagen helps a hangover, and what actually makes a difference to skin if you drink.

**The quick rules:** It's fine to take collagen on days you drink. Don't expect it to protect your skin or liver from alcohol. If skin aging is your concern, the biggest levers are drinking less, sleeping well, daily sunscreen, not smoking, and eating enough protein and vitamin C. Collagen is an optional extra on top of those, not a substitute for them.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor, dermatologist, or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before starting collagen if** you have kidney disease, are on a protein-restricted diet, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a fish, shellfish, or egg allergy (many collagen products come from marine sources or contain egg-shell membrane). **See a doctor promptly if** you notice yellowing of your skin or eyes, spider-like blood vessels on your chest or face, easy bruising, red palms, or swelling in your belly or legs. Those can be signs of liver problems rather than ordinary skin aging. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Collagen Is and Why It Matters for Skin

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body. It is the main structural protein in skin, tendons, ligaments, bone, cartilage, and the walls of blood vessels. Think of it as the scaffolding that holds tissues together and gives them strength.

In skin, collagen lives in the dermis, the thick layer under the surface. Cells called **fibroblasts** produce it, mostly type I and type III collagen, and weave it into a dense mesh along with elastin (which lets skin snap back) and moisture-holding molecules like hyaluronic acid. When that mesh is dense and well organized, skin looks firm and smooth. When it thins out or becomes disorganized, you see fine lines, sagging, and a duller texture.

Your body is always building new collagen and breaking down old collagen. In your twenties, building keeps up with breakdown. From roughly your mid-twenties onward, production slowly declines each year, and in women it drops more sharply in the years after menopause as estrogen falls. On top of that natural decline, outside factors speed up breakdown. The biggest one by far is sun exposure. Smoking is another. Heavy drinking belongs on the same list.

### What your body needs to make collagen

Building collagen isn't just a matter of eating collagen. Your fibroblasts assemble it from amino acids, especially **glycine, proline, and lysine**, and the process has a few hard requirements:

- **Vitamin C.** The enzymes that stabilize the collagen strand can't work without it. This is why scurvy, severe vitamin C deficiency, causes fragile skin, bleeding gums, and wounds that won't heal.
- **Enough total protein** to supply the amino acids.
- **Minerals such as zinc and copper**, which support the enzymes involved in building and cross-linking collagen.
- **Good sleep**, when much of the body's tissue repair happens.

Keep that list in mind, because alcohol interferes with almost every item on it.

## How Alcohol Affects Collagen and Skin

There's no single "collagen-destroying" chemical reaction from alcohol. Instead, regular heavy drinking stacks up several stresses that tilt the balance toward breakdown and away from repair. Here's how each one works.

### 1. Dehydration and fluid shifts

Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. That's why you pee more when you drink. The next day your skin can look dry, dull, and more lined, because dehydrated skin shows texture more clearly. This part is temporary and mostly cosmetic, but it's the reason skin often looks noticeably worse the morning after.

Drinking also causes puffiness, especially around the eyes and face, as fluid shifts around and blood vessels dilate. Our guide to [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating) covers why that happens and how quickly it settles.

### 2. Oxidative stress from alcohol metabolism

When your liver breaks down alcohol, it first turns it into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic and reactive compound, and the process generates reactive oxygen species (often called free radicals). With regular heavy drinking, an additional enzyme system in the liver (known as CYP2E1) ramps up and produces even more of them.

Oxidative stress matters for skin because it switches on enzymes called **matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)**, which chop up collagen. Sun damage ages skin largely through this same pathway. In lab studies, exposing skin fibroblasts to alcohol or acetaldehyde increases oxidative damage and reduces their ability to make healthy collagen. Lab findings don't translate one-to-one to real people, but they fit with what we see in heavy drinkers' skin.

### 3. Inflammation

Alcohol promotes inflammation throughout the body, partly by making the gut lining leakier so bacterial by-products reach the bloodstream, and partly through acetaldehyde itself. Chronic, low-grade inflammation keeps the immune system releasing signals that also encourage collagen breakdown and slow repair. It also worsens inflammatory skin conditions. Heavy drinking is linked to flare-ups of rosacea and psoriasis, and the persistent flushing it causes can lead to permanently visible small blood vessels on the cheeks and nose. If you flush strongly when you drink, see our guide to [red face after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking).

### 4. Nutrient depletion

People who drink heavily often run low on exactly the nutrients collagen production depends on. Alcohol can reduce absorption and increase loss of several vitamins and minerals, and heavy drinkers often eat less nutritious food. Low vitamin C is common in people with high alcohol intake, and zinc deficiency is well documented in people with alcohol-related liver disease. Low protein intake adds to the problem. You can't build new scaffolding without the raw materials. Our guide to [vitamin C and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-c-and-alcohol) goes into this in more detail.

### 5. Worse sleep

Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it fragments sleep in the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. Poor sleep raises cortisol, and sustained high cortisol is associated with collagen breakdown and thinner skin. One rough night won't age you, but years of chronically poor sleep add up.

### 6. Sugar in drinks

Many cocktails, mixers, ciders, and sweet wines carry a lot of sugar. High blood sugar over time encourages a process called glycation, where sugar molecules attach to proteins like collagen and form stiff, brittle cross-links known as advanced glycation end-products (AGEs). Glycated collagen is less flexible and harder for the body to repair. This is a long-term effect of high sugar intake in general, not something unique to alcohol, but sugary drinks contribute.

## What the Research Shows About Drinking and Facial Aging

The best-known human data comes from a large survey of more than 3,000 women across several countries, published in 2019 in the *Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology*. Researchers compared women's self-reported drinking with standardized ratings of their facial aging. Women who drank heavily (around eight or more drinks a week) were more likely to show upper-face lines, puffiness under the eyes, loss of volume in the mid-face, and visible broken blood vessels than women who drank lightly or not at all.

That kind of study shows an association, not proof that alcohol alone caused the differences. People who drink heavily may also smoke more, get more sun, or sleep less. Still, the pattern lines up with the biology described above, and it matches what dermatologists commonly see. The main takeaway is that the visible effects showed up with regular heavy drinking, not with an occasional glass of wine.

For a broader look at how alcohol affects skin over the long term, see our [alcohol and skin health analysis](/never-hungover/alcohol-skin-health-anti-aging-impact-analysis-2025).

## Collagen and the Liver: The Twist Most Articles Miss

Here's an irony worth knowing. When people talk about alcohol and collagen, they usually mean alcohol reducing the good collagen in skin. But in the liver, heavy drinking causes the opposite problem: **too much collagen in the wrong place.**

When the liver is injured over and over, by years of heavy drinking for example, cells called hepatic stellate cells switch into a repair mode and start laying down collagen. In small amounts this is normal wound healing. When the injury never stops, that collagen builds up as scar tissue. This is **fibrosis**, and when the scarring becomes widespread and distorts the liver's structure, it's called **cirrhosis**. Scarred liver tissue doesn't do the liver's jobs.

To be clear, taking a collagen supplement does not cause liver scarring. The scar collagen is made by the liver's own cells in response to injury, and the collagen you swallow is digested into amino acids like any other protein. But this is a good reminder that "more collagen" isn't automatically good, and that a supplement has no effect on the liver damage process either way. If you drink heavily, a liver blood test from your doctor is far more useful than any skin supplement. Our [liver health guide](/never-hungover/liver-health-complete-guide-optimal-liver-function-protection-2025) explains what those tests measure.

## Can You Take Collagen and Drink Alcohol?

Yes. Collagen supplements are made of collagen protein broken down into smaller pieces (usually labeled "hydrolyzed collagen" or "collagen peptides"). Your gut digests them into amino acids and short peptides, just as it does with protein from food. They don't affect the enzymes that process alcohol, they don't interact with alcohol in the bloodstream, and there are no known safety problems with having them on the same day.

A few practical points:

- **Timing doesn't matter much.** Take it whenever it's easiest to stay consistent, such as in your morning coffee or a smoothie. Taking it before a night out won't shield your skin from that night's drinks.
- **Watch for collagen gummies and drinks with added sugar.** If you're already having sugary cocktails, a sugary supplement adds more.
- **Check the source if you have allergies.** Marine collagen comes from fish skin or scales. Some joint-focused products include eggshell membrane or shellfish-derived ingredients.
- **Some products are "beauty blends."** Many collagen powders add biotin, hyaluronic acid, or vitamin C. Vitamin C is a sensible pairing because collagen production needs it. If you also take a separate multivitamin, check that you're not doubling up on anything. See our guide on [multivitamins and alcohol](/never-hungover/multivitamin-and-alcohol).
- **Medical conditions.** If you have kidney disease or have been told to limit protein, check with your doctor first, since collagen adds to your total protein intake.

## Does Collagen Actually Work? What the Supplement Research Shows

This is where it's worth being clear-eyed. The marketing around collagen is loud, and the evidence is real but modest.

**Skin.** Several randomized controlled trials of oral hydrolyzed collagen peptides, usually in doses of around 2.5 to 10 grams a day for 8 to 12 weeks, have reported improvements in skin hydration, elasticity, and in some cases the appearance of fine lines, compared with a placebo. Meta-analyses pooling these trials have generally found small but measurable benefits. The main caveats are that many of the trials were funded by companies that sell collagen, the studies are mostly small and short, and some analyses have found that the benefit looks smaller when you focus on independently funded, higher-quality studies.

**How could it work if it's digested?** It's a fair question. Most of it does get broken down into amino acids. But some small collagen fragments (dipeptides like prolyl-hydroxyproline) survive digestion and reach the bloodstream, and lab research suggests they may signal fibroblasts to produce more collagen. That's a plausible mechanism, not a settled one.

**Joints and bones.** There's some trial evidence that collagen supplements may modestly ease joint pain in people with osteoarthritis or in athletes, and a few studies on bone density, but the overall picture is less consistent than for skin.

**What collagen does not do.** It doesn't block alcohol's effects. It doesn't protect the liver. It doesn't prevent hangovers. And there's no good evidence that it offsets the skin effects of regular heavy drinking, because no trials have tested that.

A sensible way to think about it: collagen is a reasonable protein supplement that may give a small boost to skin quality over a few months. It's not a shield, and it's a distant second to the basics below.

## Does Collagen Help a Hangover?

There is no good evidence that collagen prevents or relieves a hangover. A collagen drink the morning after does give you some protein and fluid, which can make you feel slightly better, but so would breakfast and a big glass of water.

You might see claims online about glycine, an amino acid that makes up roughly a third of collagen. Some animal studies have found that glycine may reduce alcohol-related liver injury or slow alcohol absorption from the stomach. Those are rodent studies using doses and conditions that don't easily translate to a scoop of powder, and they haven't been confirmed in human hangover trials. It's an interesting research thread, not a reason to use collagen as a hangover remedy.

If you want something for the morning after, eating a meal with protein, rehydrating, and sleeping are the steps with the most support. Our article on [protein shakes for a hangover](/never-hungover/protein-shake-for-hangover) covers when a shake helps and when it doesn't, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## What Actually Helps Your Skin If You Drink

If you're reading about collagen because you're worried about what drinking is doing to your face, these are the steps that do the most, roughly in order of impact.

### Drink less, and less often

This is the single biggest factor you control besides sun exposure. The facial-aging association above showed up with heavy, regular drinking. Spacing drinks out, having alcohol-free days during the week, and alternating each drink with a glass of water all reduce the load. Many people find that cutting back from daily drinking to a few nights a week makes a visible difference within weeks, mostly in puffiness and redness.

### Protect your skin from the sun every day

Sun exposure is the leading cause of collagen breakdown in facial skin. A broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher every day does more for collagen than any supplement. If you drink at outdoor events, keep reapplying, because people tend to forget when they're drinking.

### Sleep

Give yourself a full night after drinking where you can, and try to stop drinking a few hours before bed so alcohol has a chance to clear before you sleep. Better sleep supports skin repair and lowers cortisol.

### Eat enough protein and vitamin C

Your body builds collagen from the protein you eat, and it needs vitamin C to do it. Meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, and lentils supply the amino acids. Citrus fruits, berries, kiwi, peppers, broccoli, and tomatoes supply vitamin C. If your diet is good, you're already covering most of what a collagen supplement provides.

### Don't smoke, especially while drinking

Smoking is one of the strongest drivers of skin aging, and many people smoke more when they drink. Combining the two is especially hard on skin.

### Use proven topical treatments

For people who want to go further, topical retinoids (such as prescription tretinoin) have strong evidence for stimulating collagen in sun-damaged skin. A dermatologist can advise you on what suits your skin.

### Then, optionally, collagen

If you've covered the basics and want to try a collagen supplement, give it at least 8 to 12 weeks at a consistent daily dose before judging whether it's doing anything. Choose a product that lists the dose of collagen peptides clearly and, ideally, has third-party testing.

## How Quickly Does Skin Recover After Cutting Back?

It depends on which change you're looking at.

- **Puffiness, dryness, and flushing** are driven by fluid shifts and blood vessels, so they often settle within days to a couple of weeks of drinking less.
- **Skin tone and texture** may look better within a few weeks as sleep, hydration, and inflammation improve.
- **Firmness and fine lines** depend on collagen, which your skin rebuilds slowly. Improvements, where they happen, tend to take months.
- **Broken capillaries and deep lines** may not fully reverse on their own. Dermatology treatments such as vascular lasers can help with visible blood vessels.

Skin is forgiving, but it's slow. The earlier you cut back, the more there is to preserve.

## When to See a Doctor

Most skin changes linked to drinking are cosmetic and gradual. But some skin signs point to something more serious going on with the liver, and they deserve a prompt medical visit rather than a new supplement:

- Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes (jaundice)
- Small spider-shaped blood vessels, especially on the chest, shoulders, or face
- Unusually red palms
- Bruising easily or bleeding that's slow to stop
- Persistent itching without a rash. See our guide to [itchy skin after drinking](/never-hungover/itchy-skin-after-drinking)
- Swelling of the belly, ankles, or legs
- Ongoing fatigue, loss of appetite, or pain under the right ribs

Also see a doctor if you're drinking heavily most days and want to cut back. If you get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or have trouble sleeping when you skip a day, those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal. Stopping suddenly after long-term heavy drinking can be risky, so talk to a doctor about doing it safely. If you notice confusion, hallucinations, or seizures, call 911.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It is not a skin supplement, and there is no good evidence that it protects your skin's collagen from alcohol. Its appeal for social drinkers is about how they feel the next day and general liver support, and the human evidence on that is still early.

If you want to try it alongside sensible drinking habits, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. No supplement, DHM or collagen, replaces drinking less.
If you're comparing supplements people take around drinking, see our guides to [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol), [L-theanine and alcohol](/never-hungover/l-theanine-and-alcohol), [ashwagandha and alcohol](/never-hungover/ashwagandha-and-alcohol), [NAC and alcohol](/never-hungover/nac-and-alcohol), and [L-glutamine and alcohol](/never-hungover/l-glutamine-and-alcohol).

## The Bottom Line

Collagen and alcohol are safe to combine, and there's no interaction to worry about. But collagen won't cancel out the effects of regular heavy drinking on your skin. Alcohol speeds up collagen loss through dehydration, oxidative stress, inflammation, poor sleep, and nutrient depletion, and those effects build over years. Collagen supplements may give a small, real improvement in skin hydration and elasticity over a couple of months, but the evidence is modest and often industry-funded. If you care about your skin, drink less, wear sunscreen, sleep well, eat enough protein and vitamin C, and treat collagen as an optional extra.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take collagen and drink alcohol?**

Yes. There is no known harmful interaction between collagen supplements and alcohol for healthy adults. Collagen is a food protein that your gut breaks down into amino acids and small peptides, and it does not change how your liver processes alcohol. The real issue is that regular heavy drinking works against the skin and connective-tissue benefits people take collagen for, so the supplement and the drinking pull in opposite directions.

**Does alcohol break down collagen?**

Not directly in a single night. Alcohol does not dissolve collagen. Over time, though, regular heavy drinking creates conditions that speed up collagen loss: oxidative stress from alcohol metabolism, ongoing inflammation, poorer nutrition (including lower vitamin C, which collagen production depends on), and worse sleep. Those factors raise the activity of enzymes that break collagen down and slow the cells that build it.

**Does alcohol stop collagen production?**

Moderate drinking does not stop it. Heavy, regular drinking can slow it down, mainly because the body needs vitamin C, protein, zinc, and good sleep to build collagen, and heavy drinkers often run low on all of them. Lab studies also show that alcohol and its by-product acetaldehyde stress the skin cells (fibroblasts) that make collagen. The effect builds up over months and years, not from one night out.

**Does collagen help with a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that collagen prevents or treats hangovers. A collagen drink the morning after gives you some protein and, if it is a powder mixed in water, some fluid, which can help you feel a little better. But it does nothing for the main drivers of a hangover, such as acetaldehyde, poor sleep, and inflammation. Water, food, sleep, and drinking less the night before matter far more.

**Will collagen reverse skin damage from drinking?**

It will not undo it on its own. Some controlled trials of hydrolyzed collagen peptides found modest improvements in skin hydration and elasticity after about 8 to 12 weeks, though many were funded by supplement makers. If you keep drinking heavily, those small gains are likely to be outweighed. Cutting back on alcohol, sleeping well, wearing sunscreen, and not smoking do more for skin than any supplement.

**How long after cutting back on alcohol does skin improve?**

Many people notice less puffiness and redness within a week or two, because those changes are driven by fluid shifts and blood vessel dilation, which settle quickly. Changes that depend on collagen, such as firmness and fine lines, take longer, usually months, because skin rebuilds its collagen slowly. Broken capillaries and deep lines may not fully reverse.

**Should I take collagen before or after drinking?**

Timing around drinking does not matter much, because collagen does not interact with alcohol. If you take it, pick a consistent time each day, such as in your morning coffee or a smoothie. Taking it before drinking will not protect your skin or liver from that night's alcohol.

**Is collagen bad for your liver if you drink?**

Collagen supplements are not known to harm the liver at normal doses. The liver concern runs the other way: when the liver is injured by years of heavy drinking, it lays down excess scar collagen, which is what fibrosis and cirrhosis are. A collagen supplement does not cause or worsen that process, and it does not protect against it either. If you drink heavily, ask your doctor about liver blood tests.
